newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Record diesel sales absorb Singapore storage space.
newsitem.headline: Record diesel sales absorb Singapore storage space.

text.p: Spot oil storage space in Singapore is running out following record volume of diesel sales as traders book space to cash in on the soaring business, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Some terminal operators in Singapore, said they had turned down some customers as all their spaces have been committed.
Singapore has the largest independent storage facility in Asia-Pacific with more than 3.5 million cubic meters of capacity,
"Yes, I had to turn away some customers," one terminal operator said.
As a result of the strong demand, prices for spot clean product storage space have more than doubled.
But most of these available spaces are actually being sublet by fellow traders who have leased long term storage space rather than by the terminal operators themselves, the sources said.
"We have not raised prices simply because the demand is very good as our business is based on long term relationship, and we are not going to take advantage of the situation," one operator said.
Companies who have the extra space are now asking for between 40 and 50 cents per barrel, compared to about 15 cents about one month ago, traders said.
Terminal operators said that about 80-percent of their business is sealed up in long term contracts but they are not complaining as the active trade has raised the terminal throughput.

Of the estimated three-million-cubic-metre storage space, about 70 percent is dedicated for the storage of clean petroleum products such as diesel, kerosene, gasoline and naphtha. The remainder is used to store dirty products such as fuel oil.
One company that still has space for spot oil products, said it is looking to lease around 30,000 cubic metres at 50 cents per barrel.
The surge in demand for storage space was spurred by the record volumes of diesel trade in Singapore which were done on a free-on-board (fob) basis.
Such sales require the seller to have the oil available for loading from a terminal that is stored in Singapore's many onshore tanks.
Trading sources said traders are keen to sell on an fob basis as they are able to get the best price through such sales compared to those sold on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis.
The fob sales, done on a fixed-price basis, is currently valued at about $1.00 per barrel above the prevailing spot price when hedged in the local swaps market.
Compared to this, the floating price deals for c-and-f cargoes are done at about 35 cents above prevailing spot prices.
"If possible, we try not to sell on a c-and-f basis as the fob market is much better," one trader said.
But some traders, who have not been able to get storage, have been forced to sell on a c-and-f basis in recent days.

The storage tightness would have been more severely stretched if the buyers of all the diesel cargoes, totalling more than 13 million barrels for lifting in April and May, was also storing them in the Singapore tanks.
But the traders are storing the cargoes in floating storages outside Singapore for eventual transhipment.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3093)
